s0103.literal: [jiang], [7] all are permitted to turn themselves in with grace and receive a general pardon together."
s0103.idiomatic: [generals] [7] may all surrender with clemency and share in a general amnesty."

s0104.literal: Earlier, an edict had also sent Minister of Works Xu Du with Yang Wentong and others to march out from Ancheng by land route into eastern Xiang to strike Jiao from the rear.
s0104.idiomatic: Earlier an edict had also sent Xu Du, minister of works, with Yang Wentong and others out from Ancheng overland through eastern Xiang to hit Jiao from behind.

s0105.literal: At that time Jiao had drawn up his battle line at White Snail in Ba commandery, arraying his fleet to face the royal army in stalemate without decision.
s0105.idiomatic: Jiao then held his line at White Snail in Ba commandery, his ships drawn up against the imperial fleet in an unresolved standoff.

s0106.literal: When he heard that Xu Du was pressing toward Xiangzhou, he then led his troops down from Ba and Ying with a favoring wind to give battle.
s0106.idiomatic: Learning that Xu Du was marching on Xiangzhou, he took his army down from Ba and Ying with a fair wind and joined battle.

s0107.literal: Chunyu Liang, Wu Mingche, and others recruited small boats from among the troops, richly rewarded them with gold and silver, and ordered them out first to meet the rebels' great ships and take their ramming blows.
s0107.idiomatic: Chunyu Liang and Wu Mingche raised small boats from the ranks, paid them well in gold and silver, and sent them out first to take the enemy great ships' ramming blows.

s0108.literal: When the rebel ships had exhausted all their rams, the government forces then struck them with great ships; the rebel ships were all smashed and sank in midstream.
s0108.idiomatic: Once the rebel ships had spent their rams, the imperial great ships rammed them; every rebel vessel was broken and went down mid-river.

s0109.literal: The rebels again loaded great ships with firewood and, riding the wind, set fire; soon the wind turned and burned them instead, and the rebel army suffered a great defeat.
s0109.idiomatic: The rebels then packed great ships with fuel and tried to burn the fleet downwind; the wind swung back and set their own ships ablaze, and they were routed.

s0110.literal: Jiao then fled with Dai Sengshuo in a single boat; passing Baling he did not dare enter the city and went straight to Jiangling.
s0110.idiomatic: Jiao fled with Dai Sengshuo in one boat; at Baling he dared not enter the walls and ran straight for Jiangling.

s0111.literal: Tuoba Ding and the others had no boats left to cross; they went on foot toward Baling, but the walled towns of Baling were already held by the government army, so they turned toward Xiangzhou.
s0111.idiomatic: Tuoba Ding and his men had no ships to cross with and marched on Baling on foot; the Baling towns were already in imperial hands, so they headed for Xiangzhou.

s0112.literal: Reaching the river mouth they could not cross; their food was nearly gone, and they came to the army to surrender.
s0112.idiomatic: At the river mouth they could not get across; with provisions almost gone they came in and surrendered.

s0113.literal: More than ten thousand were captured, with over four thousand horses, and sent to the capital.
s0113.idiomatic: More than ten thousand prisoners and four thousand-odd horses were sent to the capital.

s0114.literal: Jiao's partisans Cao Qing, Qian Ming, Pan Zhiquan, Lu Xian, Xi Huilüe, and more than forty others were all executed; only Ren Mannu, Zhang Zhaoyu, Cao Xuan, and Liu Guangye were spared.
s0114.idiomatic: Jiao's followers Cao Qing, Qian Ming, Pan Zhiquan, Lu Xian, Xi Huilüe, and more than forty others were put to death; only Ren Mannu, Zhang Zhaoyu, Cao Xuan, and Liu Guangye were pardoned.

s0115.literal: Dai Sengshuo was a man of Qiantang in Wu commandery.
s0115.idiomatic: Dai Sengshuo was from Qiantang in Wu commandery.

s0116.literal: He had physical strength, was brave and skilled in battle, and his clansman the Right General Sengxi greatly loved him.
s0116.idiomatic: Powerful, bold, and a capable fighter, he was much favored by his kinsman Sengxi, right general.

s0117.literal: When Sengxi grew old, on campaigns he always had Sengshuo lead the troops.
s0117.idiomatic: As Sengxi aged, he regularly put Sengshuo in command on campaign.

s0118.literal: He had merit in pacifying Wang Lin.
s0118.idiomatic: He earned merit in the campaign that pacified Wang Lin.

s0119.literal: When Sengxi died, he succeeded him as Administrator of South Danyang and garrisoned at Caishi.
s0119.idiomatic: After Sengxi's death he replaced him as administrator of South Danyang and held Caishi.

s0120.literal: On the campaign against Liu Yi, Hou Andu came out to fight from below the cliff and was cut down by the rebels; Sengshuo went on foot alone with a single blade to rescue him.
s0120.idiomatic: Campaigning against Liu Yi, Hou Andu fought the enemy below the cliff and was wounded; Sengshuo went in alone on foot with one sword to pull him out.

s0121.literal: For his merit he was made Trustworthy Martial General and Inspector of North Jiangzhou, holding concurrently the post of Administrator of Nanling.
s0121.idiomatic: For this he was made trustworthy-martial general and inspector of North Jiangzhou, and also administrator of Nanling.

s0122.literal: He again followed on the campaign against Zhou Di with merit, was transferred to Administrator of Ba commandery, and his credentials and general's title remained as before.
s0122.idiomatic: He campaigned again against Zhou Di with merit, was moved to administrator of Ba commandery, and kept his staff and general's rank.

s0123.literal: At this time he joined Jiao in rebellion and was executed at Jiangling.
s0123.idiomatic: He then rebelled with Jiao and was executed at Jiangling.

s0124.literal: Cao Qing had originally been a Wang Lin general; Xiao Zhuang falsely appointed him Left Guard General and Inspector of Wu commandery, and his command ranked below Pan Chuntuo's.
s0124.idiomatic: Cao Qing had been one of Wang Lin's generals; the puppet ruler Xiao Zhuang made him left guard general and inspector of Wu commandery, ranking below Pan Chuntuo.

s0125.literal: When Lin was defeated, Emperor Wen assigned him to Jiao; he rose to Administrator of Changsha.
s0125.idiomatic: After Lin's defeat Emperor Wen placed him under Jiao; he rose to administrator of Changsha.

s0126.literal: Qian Ming had originally been a chief commander under the Founder; afterward he successively held governorships in the Xiang region.
s0126.idiomatic: Qian Ming had once been a chief commander under the Founder and later held several posts as prefect in the Xiang region.

s0127.literal: Pan Zhiquan was Chuntuo's son; from youth he had ambition and resolve, and at twenty he became Inner Administrator of Baling.
s0127.idiomatic: Pan Zhiquan was Chuntuo's son—spirited from youth and made inner administrator of Baling at twenty.

s0128.literal: Lu Xian was a man of Qiantang in Wu commandery.
s0128.idiomatic: Lu Xian was from Qiantang in Wu commandery.

s0129.literal: Xi Huilüe was a man of Anding.

s0130.literal: Xian had originally been a Zhang Biao chief commander, and Huilüe a Wang Lin subordinate; Emperor Wen assigned both to Jiao, and each rose to a commandery governorship.
s0130.idiomatic: Xian had served Zhang Biao as chief commander and Huilüe had been under Wang Lin; Emperor Wen gave both to Jiao, and each became a commandery governor.

s0132.literal: Zhang Zhaoyu was Zhaoda's younger brother;
s0132.idiomatic: Zhang Zhaoyu was Zhaoda's younger brother;

s0133.literal: Liu Guangye was Guangde's younger brother;
s0133.idiomatic: Liu Guangye was Guangde's younger brother;

s0134.literal: Cao Xuan was an old minister of the Founder;
s0134.idiomatic: Cao Xuan was an old minister of the Founder;

s0135.literal: Ren Mannu had once sent a secret memorial to the court;
s0135.idiomatic: Ren Mannu had once sent a secret memorial to the court;

s0136.literal: for this reason they all received pardon.
s0136.idiomatic: for which they were all spared.

s0137.literal: The historian says: Although Han Zigao and Hua Jiao were but petty vessels and the lowest ranks of servitors, Emperor Wen, discerning how the ancients gained men and remedying the urgent ills of his own day, applied the art of keen sight and clear hearing and the policy of settling the people and harmonizing the masses—entrusting them with his inmost counsel without regard to pedigree.
s0137.idiomatic: The historian writes: Han Zigao and Hua Jiao were trifling men of humble birth, yet Emperor Wen—seeing how past ages chose talent and how pressing his own troubles were—used sharp judgment and policies that calmed the realm, and gave them his full trust without asking after their pedigrees.

s0138.literal: Jiao early took part in intimate service, [8] once shared in hardship and peril, knew that he had no concealment, and was rewarded with full exertion; there was the sincerity of one trusted, not ground for suspicion.
s0138.idiomatic: Jiao had long served him closely [8], had shared danger, and showed he had nothing to hide; the emperor repaid him with full trust—grounds for confidence, not for doubt.

s0139.literal: Jiao held the upper Yangtze and was loyal to Emperor Wen.
s0139.idiomatic: Jiao held the upper river and had been loyal to Emperor Wen.

s0140.literal: Dao Zhongju and Zigao likewise did not fall short in the duty of a subject.
s0140.idiomatic: Dao Zhongju and Zigao, too, had not failed in subject's duty.

s0142.literal: Zhou Wenyü garrisoned the North Suburb Xiang
s0142.idiomatic: On "Zhou Wenyü garrisoned the North Suburb Xiang"

s0146.literal: and the main biography in the History of the Southern Dynasties and
s0146.idiomatic: and the main biography in the History of the Southern Dynasties and

s0149.literal: Biao's general Shen Jin again surrendered—"Shen Jin" (jin, silken cord) in the History of the Southern Dynasties, 〈Biography of Zhang Biao〉, reads "Shen Jin" (jin, advance).
s0149.idiomatic: On "Biao's general Shen Jin again surrendered": the History of the Southern Dynasties, 〈Biography of Zhang Biao〉, reads Shen Jin (advance) for Shen Jin (silken cord).

s0150.literal: In the Liang era he was a clerical aide in the Masters of Writing Bureau for Comparison— the graph bi (compare) was originally a blank in the ink; it is supplied according to various editions.
s0150.idiomatic: On "in the Liang era he was a clerical aide in the masters of writing bureau for comparison": the graph bi was originally blank in the ink and is supplied from other editions.

s0151.literal: Changed in enfeoffment to Marquis of Chong'an county—"Marquis" in the History of the Southern Dynasties reads "Duke."
s0151.idiomatic: On "changed in enfeoffment to Marquis of Chong'an county": the History of the Southern Dynasties reads duke for marquis.

s0152.literal: He also ordered Acting-with-Staff Crown Martial General Yang Wentong to set out separately from An
s0152.idiomatic: On "he also ordered acting-with-staff crown martial general Yang Wentong to set out separately from An"

s0154.literal: [cheng], marching by land route out through Chaling—changed according to the Comprehensive Mirror.
s0154.idiomatic: On "[cheng], marching by land route out through Chaling"—emended per the Comprehensive Mirror.

s0155.idiomatic: The passage below also reads Ancheng.

s0157.literal: [Gui]yang Administrator Cao Xuan—changed according to the History of the Southern Dynasties and the Comprehensive Mirror.
s0157.idiomatic: On "[Gui]yang Administrator Cao Xuan"—emended per the History of the Southern Dynasties and the Comprehensive Mirror.

s0160.literal: [jiang]—changed according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0160.idiomatic: On "[jiang]"—emended per the History of the Southern Dynasties.

s0161.literal: Jiao early took part in intimate service—Zhang Senkai
s0161.idiomatic: On "Jiao early took part in intimate service"—Zhang Senkai

s0163.literal: says: "'Jiao' should probably read 'Zhongju,' because this discussion ought not to omit Zhongju.
s0163.idiomatic: writes: "'Jiao' should probably read 'Zhongju,' for this passage ought not to leave out Zhongju.

s0165.literal: Below it says "Jiao held the upper Yangtze and was loyal to Emperor Wen"—only then does the discussion turn to Hua Jiao.
s0165.idiomatic: Below, "Jiao held the upper river and was loyal to Emperor Wen" is where Hua Jiao is first discussed in earnest.
